fact: Motz, an infill maker, separates texturized putting greens, about half an inch tall with about 1.5 to 2.5 pounds of infill per square foot, from sand-filled greens, 1 to 1 1/4 inches tall with as much as 4 to 6 pounds of raw sand per square foot under a top dressing of about half a pound to a pound of coated sand.
quote: For putting green applications, it’s important to understand the difference between a texturized installation and a sand-filled installation. A texturized putting green is manufactured with a short pile height of about half an inch, using about 1.5-2.5 lbs. of Envirofill 30/50 per square foot. A sand-filled putting green is manufactured with a taller 1”- 1 1/4” pile height and demands more infill — as much as 4-6 lbs per square foot of round raw sand ballast topped with ½-1lb of 16/30 Envirofill per square foot.
source_label: Motz, "How Many Pounds of Infill Do You Need per Square Foot of Turf?" (2018, updated Dec. 20, 2024)
notes: Motz sells coated-sand infill (Envirofill), so the infill figures are a seller's recommendation. The quote is the page as rendered; a plain-text strip adds a space before the comma after the linked words "putting green applications".

fact: Motz says a recreational (texturized) green has much less chipping distance because it has less sand and cushion for the ball to grab, so a ball chipped from too far bounces off, while a professional-style sand-filled green can take chips from up to 50 or even 100 yards.
quote: Recreational: The chipping distance is much shorter on this type of green because there’s less sand and less cushion layer for the ball to grab. The result is a ball that bounces off of the green if you are chipping from too far away. Professional: The chipping distance on a professional-style putting green can extend up to 50 or even 100 yards whereas a recreational green will mostly be used for practice immediately around the green.
source_label: Motz, "How to Choose the Best Artificial Grass for a Putting Green" (2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: Section "#1: Chipping distance of an artificial putting green". Motz's "professional" style is the sand-filled, 1 to 1 1/4 inch system it describes in its infill-pounds post; "recreational" is the crimped, texturized green.

fact: Motz says a recreational green's crimped, texturized fibers make it easier to maintain, with no routine rolling, while a professional-style green has to be rolled extensively at install and needs more grooming, brushing and leveling of its infill over time.
quote: Recreational: Synthetic turf putting greens used for leisure are easier to maintain than professional-level greens because the turf fibers are crimped (textured). There’s no routine maintenance to roll the turf, since you can’t adjust the turf fiber on this type of system. Professional: On professional-style greens, the turf will need to be rolled extensively before completing the system. … Competitive players are usually more meticulous and their greens endure more usage, meaning a professional-level green is going to require more surface grooming, brushing, and leveling out of the infill layers over time.
source_label: Motz, "How to Choose the Best Artificial Grass for a Putting Green" (2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: Section "#2 Maintenance of an artificial putting green".

fact: Motz puts a recreational green at about 8 to 11 on the stimpmeter with two to four pounds of infill per square foot, and a professional-style green at about 10 to 13 with five to seven pounds of ballast per square foot.
quote: Recreational: When it comes to speed, the average ball speed will likely be 8-11 stimp on recreational putting green turf. Professional: On professional-style greens, the stimp rating is likely to increase to 10-13. … Professional-style putting greens require a ballast, five to seven pounds of turf infill per square foot. … If you’re building a recreational putting green, you can plan to use two to four pounds of Envirofill per square foot.
source_label: Motz, "How to Choose the Best Artificial Grass for a Putting Green" (2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: Sections "#3 Stimp" and "What infill should I use". The same post quotes third-party installed prices; this page uses none of them.

fact: Motz says a professional-level backyard putting green generally costs 20 to 50% more than one built for leisure, largely because of the type and amount of materials.
quote: The pricing fluctuation largely comes down to the type and amount of materials used — in the next section, we’ll answer the age-old question: which is better, nylon or poly putting greens? — but in general, a professional-level backyard putting green will cost you anywhere from 20 to 50% more than one made for leisure.
source_label: Motz, "How to Choose the Best Artificial Grass for a Putting Green" (2020, updated May 15, 2024)
notes: Section "#4 Cost". The same paragraph quotes third-party dollar figures; this guide uses only the percentage, and no prices.

fact: Motz says a longer-pile polypropylene 'bent grass' green lets golfers adjust its speed and chip from greater distances, while a low-pile or texturized nylon green gives consistency but not as much speed or flexibility.
quote: A longer pile, polypropylene “bent grass” system is typically selected by those golfers who desire more flexibility with how they will use the green. These will allow you to adjust the speed of the surface, chip from greater distances, and promote an overall closer comparison to a natural green, without all of the maintenance of course. A low-pile or texturized nylon product will provide consistency but, not as much speed or flexibility.
source_label: Motz, "Small Infill, Big Impact for Putting Greens" (2016, updated Nov. 21, 2022)

fact: SYNLawn Golf, which sells nylon greens, says its nylon greens are mostly fiber with very little sand, while a polypropylene green is mostly sand, hard to keep consistent, has to be replenished, and its sand grows harder the longer the green is used.
quote: The putting green is mostly sand which makes it very difficult to maintain consistent performance. … Nylon putting greens offer a great deal of flexibility during installation because they are mostly fiber with very little use of sand. … Due to the large amount of sand used for polypropylene greens, it is necessary that they are replenished to maintain proper infill levels. The longer a polypropylene green is in use the harder the sand will become. Periodic maintenance will be required to maintain proper performance levels.
source_label: SYNLawn Golf, "The Nylon Advantage" (manufacturer page, updated July 2, 2026)
notes: Marketing by a nylon-green seller comparing its own product with polypropylene sand-filled greens; the page describes testing but publishes no data. nylon-vs-polyethylene-turf cites the same page for the sand line only.

fact: SYNLawn Golf says approach shots hold on a polypropylene sand green but the ball dies on impact, and that chips to its nylon greens check and roll closer to a natural green.
quote: Approach shots will hold on a polypropylene green, however the ball dies on impact and does not match the performance of a natural putting green. … Balls chipped to a nylon putting green check and roll much closer to the performance of natural putting greens. … Balls chipped to a polypropylene green slowed abruptly and the roll to the hole was inconsistent (off-line) compared to a natural grass putting green.
source_label: SYNLawn Golf, "The Nylon Advantage" (manufacturer page, updated July 2, 2026)
notes: A seller's claims about its own product against a competing type.

fact: SYNLawn Golf's Classic Putt is a 1/2-inch, 34-ounce nylon green with no thatch zone that the maker rates at 9 to 10 on the stimpmeter and says holds shots from inside 150 yards when paired with its TrueStop underlayment.
quote: This nylon putting green turf delivers Stimp 9-10 green speeds, realistic check and bounce, and TrueStop™ shot reception … Paired with SYNLawn’s exclusive TrueStop™ underlayment system, Classic Putt becomes a complete short game environment, accepting and holding shots inside 150 yards … Finished Pile Height 1/2” Finished Pile Weight 34 oz. … Grass Zone Yarn/Color Nylon / Verde … Thatch Zone Yarn/Color -
source_label: SYNLawn Golf, Classic Putt product page (updated May 31, 2026)
notes: The same page lists permeability of more than 150 inches per hour and a 60 oz total weight; this guide does not use them.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's True Putt, a sand-filled green, is slit-film polypropylene about 1.00 inch tall with a 35-ounce face weight and no thatch color listed, and calls for 4 to 6 pounds of infill per square foot.
quote: Type: Slit Film … Composition/Structure: PP … Pile/Face Weight: Approx. 35 Ounces … Pile Height: Approx. 1.00 Inches … Thatch Color: N/A … Weight: 4-6 Lbs Per Sq Ft*
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, True Putt spec sheet (REV112425)
notes: The infill weight sits under the sheet's "Particulate Infill" heading. "Sand-filled" is Motz's term for this build (1 to 1 1/4 inch pile, 4 to 6 lb); SGW's own column calls True Putt tournament quality, slit film.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's Nylon Putt 2-Tone is texturized nylon about 0.50 inches tall with a 36-ounce face weight and no thatch color listed, calls for 2.0 to 3.0 pounds of infill per square foot, and gives the care line "Rinse and groom as needed to limit matting."
quote: Type: Texturized Nylon … Pile/Face Weight: Approx. 36 Ounces … Pile Height: Approx. 0.50 Inches … Thatch Color: N/A … Weight: 2.0-3.0 Lbs Per Sq Ft* … Rinse and groom as needed to limit matting
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Nylon Putt 2-Tone spec sheet (REV112425)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says nylon and textured polyethylene putting greens still need infill placed from the bottom of the fibers to the top of the finished surface, and recommends rolling after infill so the green has equal stimpmeter speeds.
quote: Nylon and textured PE putting greens need infill to be placed internally from the bottom to the top of the finished surface … I recommend pressure rolling after the infill is complete. This will allow the fibers to be pressed down to the infill height and create a smooth surface for the ball to roll on. This compression will create equal Stimpmeter speeds.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Perfecting Putting Green Surfaces, Part 2: Infill Placement (April 14, 2020)
notes: Installer column from a turf distributor, written for installers.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says sand should not go into wet putting green turf, because moisture holds the sand on the fibers instead of letting it drop to the base, and recommends drying the surface with a backpack leaf blower first if the work cannot wait.
quote: When moisture meets synthetic turf fibers, it sticks to the fibers and prevents infill from dropping into the base of the synthetic turf. Moisture can prevent infill from doing its job. … If you must get the job done due to time constraints and/or installation deadlines, you must dry out the turf in order for the infill to penetrate to the bottom. I recommend using a high-powered backpack leaf blower to dry out the entire surface prior to placing infill.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Perfecting Putting Green Surfaces, Part 2: Infill Placement (April 14, 2020)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says a typical texturized green is about half an inch thick and takes two to four pounds of infill per square foot that must be kept up or the green can move and wrinkle, while its slit-film True Putt takes four to six pounds and may need to be groomed and refilled if the infill runs low.
quote: A typical texturized synthetic turf putting green averages around ½ inch in thickness and requires between two and four pounds of infill per square foot. … Infill levels must be maintained on texturized putting green materials or damage may occur along with movement and wrinkles. … This product acts much like real bent grass and requires four to six pounds of infill per square foot. If the Infill becomes depleted, the True Putt may need to be defibrillated and Infill replenished.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Infill Maintenance (Oct. 22, 2020, updated Apr. 2, 2025)
notes: "Defibrillated" is the column's word for fibrillating (brushing up) the slit-film yarn; the fact says groomed.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says rain, snow, sleet and hail can deplete infill on all synthetic turf, that repeated flooding means measuring and replenishing it, and recommends replenishing and rolling putting greens each spring after snow or winter weather.
quote: Rain, snow, sleet, and hail can deplete infill levels on all types of synthetic turf. When continual flooding happens, Infill levels will need to be measured and replenished. … I also recommend replenishing and rolling putting greens in the spring after snow fall and/or winter conditions.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Infill Maintenance (Oct. 22, 2020, updated Apr. 2, 2025)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says most putting green turf is made without drainage holes because water running into the base can soften it and ruin the contours, so a green needs slope and base design to shed storm water, and a flat green can trap water at the fringe and air-lock into wrinkles.
quote: most putting green materials are manufactured without drainage holes punched into the backing. … Excessive water intrusion, particularly a lot of water, can soften the base, initiate settlement, and destroy any existing planetary undulations that were created. … Now, if your green is completely flat and level, water has nowhere to go. It can get trapped by the exterior fringe, and during a heavy storm, that trapped water can cause serious issues. One of those issues is called “air-locking.”
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Why Don't Putting Greens Have Drainage Holes? (Nov. 29, 2025)
notes: Some greens are perforated (SYNLawn Golf lists more than 150 inches per hour for Classic Putt), so read the backing line on each sheet.

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says infill can wash out in heavy rain, that a leaf blower's high air pressure can displace or remove it, and that a home putting green needs periodic rolling, a low-setting blower before each use, and brushing and topping up of its infill to hold its speed.
quote: Over time, infill can get displaced from high-traffic areas or wash out from heavy rains. … Leaf Blower: A leaf blower is an effective tool for clearing leaves, pine needles, and other light debris from your turf surface. However, it should be used with caution, as high air pressure can displace or remove the infill. … Regular Rolling: To keep the surface perfectly smooth and fast, you may need to roll it with a water-filled lawn roller periodically. … Meticulous Debris Removal: Even tiny debris like seeds or small twigs can affect a putt. Use a leaf blower on a low setting daily or before each use to keep the surface immaculate. … you’ll need to brush the green regularly to keep the infill evenly distributed and may need to top it off to maintain the desired speed.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (Nov. 27, 2025, updated Sept. 5, 2026)

fact: The Colorado Climate Center describes moderate to high wind on the plains, periodic severe turbulent winds near the mountains, dry winters with strong winds, and summer thunderstorms that can drop more than 4 inches of rain in a few hours.
quote: The climate of the plains is comparatively uniform from place to place, with characteristic features of low relative humidity, abundant sunshine, infrequent rains and snow, moderate to high wind movement, and a large daily and seasonal range in temperature. … More often, winter brings dry air and strong winds contributing to the aridity of the area. … Summer precipitation over the plains comes largely from thunderstorm activity and is sometimes extremely heavy. Localized rains in excess of 4" sometimes fall in just a few hours contributing to local flooding. … areas very near the mountains are subject to periodic, severe turbulent winds from the effects of high westerly winds over the mountain barrier.
source_label: Colorado Climate Center (Colorado State University), Climate of Colorado

fact: CSU Extension notes that artificial turf collects leaves and other wind-blown dirt and debris that must be removed.
quote: The companies that sell and install these lawns insist that they are virtually maintenance free, but artificial turf collects leaves and other wind-blown dirt and debris that must somehow be removed.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1537, Artificial Turf for Lawns
notes: The page's HTML splits "dirt" around an inline image; quoted as the rendered word.

fact: Firestone's Development Code defines artificial turf as a manufactured substitute for organic turf, lawn or sod that simulates a well-maintained lawn and meets the code's quality, materials and installation standards, and says nothing about putting greens.
quote: Artificial turf. A manufactured substitute for organic turf, lawn, or sod which effectively simulates the appearance of a well-maintained lawn and meets all the quality, materials and installation standards outlined in this code.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.11.3, Terms defined: "Artificial turf" (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read 2026-09-25 through the Municode content API (jobId 488870, productId 18062). Searched all of Chapter 6 and Chapter 11 for putting, golf and sport court: the only golf entries are commercial uses (golf course; golf driving range or putting course; miniature golf), none of them a residential backyard green. Whether 16.6.4.F.2 reaches a backyard green is not settled by the text: pages say ask Firestone Planning.

fact: Firestone requires every artificial turf area to meet its standards, allows blades only of lead-free polyethylene, polypropylene, a vegetable-based product or a blend, prohibits nylon, and requires a permeable backing with holes in a grid no wider than 4 by 6 inches.
quote: Location, materials, appearance, installation, and maintenance of artificial turf areas shall comply with all requirements of this FDC. … The blade material shall be made of either lead-free polyethylene, polypropylene, vegetable based product or a blend of the three (3). Nylon or other plastic shall be prohibited. … The backing shall be permeable with holes spaced in a uniform grid pattern not to exceed four (4) inches by six (6) inches on center.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.a.i and c.i–ii (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read 2026-09-25 through the Municode content API (jobId 488870, productId 18062).

fact: Firestone requires turf to include a tan thatch layer, a pile height of 1.75 to 3 inches and a face weight of at least 70 ounces.
quote: Blade yarn colors shall mimic natural turf including green blade color(s) and include a tan thatch layer. ii. Blade pile height shall be between one and three-quarters (1.75) inches and three (3) inches. iii. Pile face weight shall be at least seventy (70) ounces.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.d (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read 2026-09-25 through the Municode content API.

fact: Firestone's code says turf infill shall be a non-toxic anti-microbial material such as silica sand or acrylic coated sand, and prohibits crumb rubber.
quote: Infill material shall be a non-toxic anti-microbial material such as silica sand or acrylic coated sand to prevent odors and bacteria formation. Crumb rubber filler shall be prohibited.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.f.v (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read 2026-09-25 through the Municode content API. The sentence governs what infill is; it does not say a turf must carry infill.
